title: Who Owns the Truth: Boundaries, Bounded Contexts and Systems of Record
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/04-boundaries-and-systems-of-record/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over below, then corrected after one end-to-end check run. It is a contract, not a description: in the places listed under open_questions the published chapter does not yet do what the spec asks.

know: What a business fact, a system of record, a copy, a writer and a bounded context are.
The four ways merchants assign ownership and when each stops fitting.
believe: Copies are unavoidable; the failure is a copy that nobody has declared to be a copy.
'Single source of truth' means one record per fact, not one system for every fact.
can_do: Write an entity–owner table for their own landscape, with a writer list and a reconciliation per row.
Tell, from the writer list, whether a claimed system of record is one.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or integration lead who inherits a landscape of connectors, and product, finance and operations leaders who are told to 'sync it both ways'.
already_knows: The order's journey and its handoffs (journey-of-an-order).
The capability map and that each capability owns a kind of fact (commerce-capability-map).
Kestrel & Pine and the Black Friday Oversell, in outline (meet-kestrel-and-pine).
does_not_know: System of record, copy, writer, bounded context, reconciliation, event.
ERP, WMS, POS, PIM, OMS, PSP beyond a first mention.

acceptance_criteria.probe: The shop shows 12 units of a jacket and the warehouse system shows 0. Using only this chapter: what are the first two questions you ask?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which system is the record for this fact; who or what can write the value in each system. Not 'how do we sync faster'.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why three systems showing three statuses for one order may all be correct.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Shop: 'Delivered'. Warehouse: 'In picking'. Finance: 'Not invoiced'. Can all three be right? Explain.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes: each system's 'order' is a different object in a different bounded context; what is missing is an owner of the view across them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can fill one row of an entity–owner table with all six columns for a fact of their choice.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Fill one row of the entity–owner table for 'consumer price'.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Record, who may write, where copies live, how copies learn, how disagreement is found; all five answered specifically.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (callouts and paragraphs p01 to p04) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Records and copies; why 'order' means different things; an entity–owner table; a comparison of ownership choices; Kestrel & Pine's stock as the worked case; vendor documentation as evidence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].
The conclusion returns to the introduction's two disagreeing statuses and says what the reader can now see in them.

thesis.question: When several systems hold the same fact (a price, a stock level, an order status, a customer), which one is right, and how do the others find out?
thesis.claim: Copies of a fact are unavoidable and harmless; unowned copies are the failure, so a merchant must name exactly one system of record per fact (not per system, and not per company), treat every other value as a copy that learns from it, and reassign that ownership when the business changes shape.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the remedy for disagreeing systems is faster two-way synchronization, or a single source of truth read as one system that holds everything.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine oversold 1,340 units on one evening while every system reported its own number honestly; without a named record, no amount of synchronization can say which number should have won.
thesis.how_why: A disagreement can be resolved only if one value is entitled to win; the writer list shows whether a record is real, bounded contexts explain why one shared model is not the answer, and each scale stage brings a new system that claims facts the previous owner held.

supporting_claims.claim: When copies disagree, the question is which value is entitled to win, not how to copy faster.
Ownership is decided per fact, and it is real only when the record has one writer and its copies have none.
The same word names different objects in different bounded contexts, so systems should share identifiers and translate at boundaries instead of sharing one model.
Ownership becomes usable as an entity–owner table whose rows also name the writers, the refresh and how disagreement is found.
Which system should be the hub depends on where orders and stock originate, so ownership must be reassigned at each stage transition.
Ownership that has been decided still erodes, and each way it erodes has a detection and a recovery.

role.contribution: Makes the part's central decision: for each fact on the capability map, which system is the record and which are copies.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene, facts-records-copies, bounded-contexts, entity-owner-table: each supplies the terms the next one uses

flow.rationale: The reader meets six honest, disagreeing numbers before any term is defined, so the vocabulary arrives as the answer to a problem they already feel. The table comes only after records, copies and contexts, because its columns are those terms. Choices, stages and failure modes follow the table because each is a way of filling it in or keeping it true. Opening with definitions would lose the newcomer; opening with the table would present columns the reader cannot yet read.

hook.content: A customer asks where a parcel is. The storefront says Delivered; the warehouse system says In picking. Is one record stale, or do the two describe different parts of the order?

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has contacted support about an order, or answered such a contact, has seen two screens disagree.
bridge.to_topic: Until someone knows which value is authoritative, copying either status faster only spreads the wrong answer; that authority is what a system of record is.

thesis_statement.text: Copies are unavoidable; unowned copies are the failure. Name one system of record per fact, decide who may change it, how copies learn and how errors are repaired.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: "Where Does Stock Live?"
sections.controlling_idea: Six people gave six honest answers to 'where does stock live', and the useful question turned out to be which of the six is right, not how to sync them faster.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the problem before the vocabulary: every number was honest, and none was entitled to win.

flow.rationale: The question, the six answers, the evening it mattered, then the decision: the reader reaches W1 the way Noor did.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's claim that a fact needs an authoritative system.
transition_in.introduces: One company and one fact, stock, where no system had that authority.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Before the Waypoint program was approved, the head of engineering asked who owned the stock figure and got six answers.

evidence.what: Who / where stock lives in their words / what the number actually is, six rows.
evidence.shows: Each answer is true of a different number, so the disagreement is structural, not a mistake by any one person.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At 20:00 on Black Friday, twenty minutes after the warehouse sold its last unit, six systems showed six quantities for one jacket.

evidence.what: Reconstruction for the Ridgewalker women's M in moss, 27 November 2026, labelled illustrative.
evidence.shows: The six answers were not only six opinions; they were six different numbers at the same moment.

transition_in.introduces: One variant at one moment under those six answers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the copying chain took up to two hours, channels sold from old figures and produced the Black Friday Oversell.

evidence.what: 1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders cancelled or delayed, about €96,000.
evidence.shows: The cost of copies that nobody had ranked.

transition_in.introduces: What selling from them cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The question that led to a decision was 'which of the six is right?', and the answer, the shelf, made the warehouse system the record and everything else a copy.

evidence.what: Waypoint decision W1: WMS for Duiven stock, POS for store stock, marketplace stock as a tracked external location, an availability service computing from the three; Figure 1.
evidence.shows: Reframing the question from speed to authority is what produced an actionable decision.

transition_in.carries_over: The two-hour chain, which invites the question 'how do we sync faster'.
transition_in.introduces: The different question that was asked.

sections.heading: Facts, Records and Copies
sections.controlling_idea: Four plain terms (fact, record, copy, writer) are enough to state ownership, and the writer list is the test of whether it is real.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the terms the thesis is stated in and the test that distinguishes a named record from a real one.

flow.rationale: Each definition uses only the ones before it: a record is defined for a fact, a copy against the record, a writer against both; the warning about 'single source of truth' needs all four.

transition_in.carries_over: The words 'record' and 'copy', used in the scene without definition.
transition_in.introduces: Their definitions, and two further terms.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four terms carry the chapter: fact, record, copy and writer.
A business fact is something the business needs to be true about the world and acts on.

evidence.what: A variant's barcode, a customer's price, 14 units in Duiven, order #1072455 has shipped.
evidence.shows: Facts are small and specific, which is why ownership is per fact.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The system of record for a fact is the one system whose value wins when copies disagree and the only one in which the fact is changed directly.

evidence.what: The bank's ledger is the record for your balance; the budgeting app holds a copy. The shelf count in the WMS against the number on the product page.
evidence.shows: The reader already accepts this ranking in everyday life.

transition_in.introduces: The system that is authoritative for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A copy is the same fact held elsewhere; copies are necessary, and the only rule is that a copy is known to be a copy and is never edited to fix a disagreement.

evidence.what: The storefront needs a stock number to render in milliseconds; the data warehouse needs every order; the marketplace needs the price.
evidence.shows: Copies exist for good reasons, so eliminating them is not the goal.

transition_in.carries_over: The record as the one authoritative value.
transition_in.introduces: Every other value, and why it is legitimate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The practical test of ownership is the writer list: if a copy has writers of its own it is a second record, and the two will diverge.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule that a copy is never edited.
transition_in.introduces: The writer, and a test that makes the rule checkable.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: 'Single source of truth' is right as one record per fact and wrong as one system for every fact.

evidence.what: No system is the natural home of both the shelf count and the ledger posting; Figure 2.
evidence.shows: The popular phrase, read literally, contradicts per-fact ownership.

transition_in.carries_over: Ownership per fact, tested by writers.
transition_in.introduces: The common phrase that sounds like the same idea and is often read as its opposite.

sections.heading: Bounded Contexts: Why the Warehouse's Order Is Not the Ledger's Order
sections.controlling_idea: The same word names different objects in different systems, so some disagreements are not stale copies at all and need translation, not a winner.

advances_thesis.how: Blocks the wrong conclusion from the previous section, that one shared model would make ownership simple.

flow.rationale: The concept and its sources first, then one order in four contexts, then the incident, then the rules that follow; the reader sees the incident as a case of the concept rather than as an anecdote.

transition_in.carries_over: Record and copy as two values of the same fact.
transition_in.introduces: Cases where two systems hold different facts under one name.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A bounded context is a boundary inside which a model and its words have one agreed meaning.

evidence.what: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003).
evidence.shows: The term and its origin.

evidence.what: Fowler: total unification of the domain model for a large system 'will not be feasible or cost-effective'; confusion recurs 'with polysemes like Customer and Product'.
evidence.shows: Practitioner authority for the claim that one model for everyone is not the remedy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The storefront, order management, the warehouse and the ERP each have their own 'order', and they are not the same object.

evidence.what: Context / what 'order' means / what it contains / its states, four rows.
evidence.shows: Side by side, the four objects visibly differ in content and in states.

transition_in.introduces: The same idea in plain words for one term, 'order'.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Three-Status Order generated 11 tickets because its three statuses described three different objects, each correctly.

evidence.what: Order #1052877: fleece shipped 7 December 2026, socks waited a week; platform 'Delivered', WMS 'In picking', ERP 'Not invoiced'.
evidence.shows: All three statuses were true of their own object; this is the introduction's puzzle, resolved.

transition_in.introduces: One order on which three of them collided.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What was missing was not a correct status but an owner of the view across contexts, which is the job of an order management system.

evidence.what: Six days without a combined view; Waypoint decision W2 assigns it to a purchased OMS.
evidence.shows: The remedy is an owner of the whole order that keeps the separate facts.

transition_in.introduces: The consequence for the customer and what resolves it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: 'Product' and 'customer' split across contexts in the same way as 'order'.

evidence.what: Product as content, PIM attributes, ERP item, WMS SKU; Eva Janssen as four unlinked customer records.
evidence.shows: The pattern is general, not a peculiarity of orders.

transition_in.introduces: Two more words with the same property.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Translate at the boundary and share identifiers rather than models.

evidence.what: The OMS-to-WMS connector turns an order into a fulfillment order; order number, SKU and GTIN let contexts refer to the same thing; Figure 3.
evidence.shows: Both rules are concrete work with an owner, not a slogan.

transition_in.carries_over: Words that legitimately mean different things per context.
transition_in.introduces: Two design rules that follow.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the definitions into the artifact the reader will produce, and adds the columns that make ownership enforceable.

flow.rationale: The whole table first, then the rows that surprise newcomers, then the one column most tables omit, then the separate question of freshness; the reader needs the whole before the exceptions make sense.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter's deliverable is a table with one row per business fact and five columns of decisions, given here for a merchant at the omnichannel stage.

evidence.what: Fourteen facts by system of record, who may write, copies live in, how copies learn, disagreement found by.
evidence.shows: The decisions are specific enough to be written per fact, and the table is short enough to maintain.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four rows carry lessons newcomers miss: stock has a record per location, availability has no human writer, payment's record is outside the company, and business and consumer customers have different records.

evidence.shows: Each lesson corresponds to an incident caused by ignoring it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A record with copies and no reconciliation is a record on trust, so every copy row needs a named way of finding disagreement.

evidence.what: The Black Friday chain ran on trust.
evidence.shows: The omitted column is the one whose absence caused the incident.

transition_in.introduces: The column most tables leave out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ownership decides who wins, not how quickly copies must follow; freshness depends on what a stale copy costs and differs sharply by fact.

transition_in.introduces: What happens when one rhythm is applied to all.

sections.heading: Four Ways to Assign Ownership
sections.controlling_idea: Merchants assign ownership in four ways, three of them decisions, and the right one is set by where orders and stock originate.

transition_in.carries_over: One recommended table for one stage.
transition_in.introduces: The other ways the same table is filled in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: There are four ways; three are decisions and the fourth is what happens without one.
With the ERP as hub, the web shop is a front end; this fits one channel and one warehouse and stops fitting when several parties need stock within minutes.

evidence.what: 'Business Central acts as the system of record for inventory', pushed one way every 15 to 30 minutes.
evidence.source: Microsoft Learn, Business Central Shopify Connector, October 2026
evidence.shows: A shipped product encodes this option and its batch rhythm.

transition_in.introduces: The first option.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With the platform as hub, its order and stock are the record; this fits a direct-to-consumer brand and stops fitting when orders or stock originate elsewhere.

transition_in.introduces: The opposite centre.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With ownership per fact and an order hub, each fact goes to the system that originates it, which keeps a sales estimate from overwriting a physical count.

transition_in.introduces: An arrangement with no single hub.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Specialist vendors describe the same boundaries, and should be read as explaining their own categories.

transition_in.introduces: Its cost and when not to pay it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With no decision, every system becomes a writer of every fact it holds; this is the default because it is never chosen.

transition_in.introduces: The one nobody chooses.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The table is rewritten at each scale stage, because each stage brings a system that claims facts the previous owner held.

evidence.shows: The decision, not faster copying of the old chain, removes the oversell window.

transition_in.introduces: Its effect on the incident the chapter opened with.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first reconciliation after the change found copies that had drifted, which is the reason every copy row has one.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Ownership decided is not ownership kept: five things erode it, each with a detection and a recovery.

advances_thesis.how: Prevents the reader from treating the table as a one-off document.

flow.rationale: Five failure modes in the same three-part shape (what happens, detection, recovery), ordered from failures in the copies to failure in the record itself, which no ownership rule fixes.

transition_in.introduces: How it stops working after it is decided.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ownership decided is not ownership kept; five things go wrong.
A second writer appears; a periodic write audit against the writer column finds it, and removing the write and re-publishing from the record repairs it.

evidence.what: The App That Wrote Stock.
evidence.shows: A named case of the failure.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A copy goes stale; a lag metric per copy finds it, and a full re-publication from the record repairs it.

evidence.what: The two-hour chain; the Deprecated Endpoint of February 2027.
evidence.shows: Staleness by design and staleness by breakage are the same failure.

transition_in.introduces: The second.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A copy is edited by hand; change logs and daily refund reconciliation find it, and routing the action through the owner repairs it.

evidence.what: The Double Refund.
evidence.shows: A well-meant manual fix is a write outside the flow.

transition_in.introduces: The third.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A copy is mistaken for the record; asking which table row a disputed number comes from finds it, and publishing the table repairs it.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The record itself is wrong; no ownership rule fixes that, and it must be corrected in the record by its own writers.

transition_in.introduces: The failure of the record.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Records, bounded contexts, the hub choice and the failure modes are one decision seen four ways: for every fact, someone must be able to say which value wins, who may change it, and how anyone would find out that a copy has drifted. The table is where that is written; the stage transition is when it is rewritten.
conclusion.so_what: A bought hub fed by unreconciled sources is one more copy, and a written table with no reconciliation is a record on trust; the reader's first step costs nothing and comes before any purchase.

callback.to: The introduction's parcel that is Delivered in one system and In picking in another.
callback.how: The reader can now say that neither status was stale: they were true of different objects, and what was missing was an owner of the view across them.

takeaway.content: Write the entity–owner table for your own landscape before buying any hub, with the writer list and the reconciliation per row, and revisit it the day a second system originates orders or counts stock. Eight questions to ask follow.

open_questions: The six-quantity reconstruction for the Ridgewalker variant at 20:00 on 27 November 2026 is labelled illustrative; journey-peak-day and inventory-and-availability may reuse or refine it.

The entity–owner table names the platform's price lists as the consumer price record; pricing-architecture may move that to a pricing engine for the omnichannel stage and should then update the row here.
Customer identity is left 'not yet decided' in the Truth-pattern table because the Waypoint decisions name no customer master; identity-and-master-data should resolve it.

decision_log.decision: Lead with 'which of the six is right?' so that the business problem (six honest answers, one oversell) precedes the vocabulary; the definitions follow the scene.
rejected: Opening with the definition of a system of record.

decision_log.decision: Use the Three-Status Order to teach bounded contexts, because order status is the case where the copies are all correct about different objects; stock is used for records and copies, where one value is simply wrong.
Keep the hub comparison to four options and cite vendors' own boundary statements (Fluent, OneStock, Microsoft), with vendor interest noted in the text.
Include the 'Across Scale Stages' section although it is optional in Part I, because the chapter's third key point is that ownership changes with scale and the table is where that is shown.
rejected: Omitting the section, as Part I permits.
